SUBJECT:  RESCISSION AND RE-ADOPTION OF MOTION TO REMOVE
  MAYOR

RECOMMENDATION

Rescind and re-adopt the City Council’s emergency motion from the July 1, 2025 meeting
to: Initiate an investigation into confidential allegations of Councilmember Loa; and
remove him from the title of “Mayor” and all committees and city assignments during the
pendency of the investigation.

DISCUSSION

On July 1, 2025, the City Council passed an emergency motion to investigate confidential
allegations of Councilmember Loa and remove him from the title of “Mayor” and all
committees and city assignments during the pendency of the investigation.

On July 8, 2025, the City Council received a letter from Councilmember Loa, complaining
of a Brown Act violation and requesting the City Council cure and correct the alleged
violation.

While the City Council acted properly, in an abundance of caution and at the request of
Councilmember Loa, it is recommended that City Council rescind and re-adopt its motion.

SUBJECT:  APPROVE REQUISITION WITH HASA, INC., FOR POOL CHEMICAL
  SUPPLIES IN AN AMOUNT NOT TO EXCEED $193,500 FOR FY
  2025-26

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Approve Requisition No. 260012 with Hasa, Inc., for pool chemical supplies in an
  amount not to exceed $193,500 for FY 2025-26; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager Pro Tem or his designee to approve Requisition No.
  260012 with Hasa, Inc., and the resulting purchase order, including minimal and/or
  non-substantial changes.

BACKGROUND

The City operates four community pools and DryTown Water Park, all of which require
ongoing maintenance to ensure public safety and water quality. Essential supplies such
as chlorine, acid, and other chemicals are necessary to maintain sanitary conditions and
meet state and county health regulations for aquatic facilities.

DISCUSSION

In March 2024, the City issued Bid No. 24-003-3400 for pool chemical supplies. Hasa,
Inc. was the lowest responsive bidder, and City Council approved a $212,500 purchase
order through June 2025. The Parks and Recreation Department now plans to extend the
purchase order contract for one more year, from July 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026. This is
the first of two available extension options.

The proposed pricing for pool chemicals aligns with current market conditions. The
requested funding amount is based on the vendor’s current price schedule, the City’s
historical chemical usage data, and projected facility needs.

SUBJECT:  APPROVE REQUISITION WITH MORGAN INGLAND LLC FOR
  COMMERCIAL STREETLIGHT POLES IN AN AMOUNT NOT TO
  EXCEED $241,080 FOR FISCAL YEAR 2025-26

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Approve Requisition No. 260001 with Morgan Ingland LLC for commercial
  streetlight poles in an amount not to exceed $241,080 for Fiscal Year 2025-26;
  and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager Pro Tem or his designee to approve the requisition
  and resulting purchase order with Morgan Ingland LLC, including minimal and/or
  non-substantial changes.

BACKGROUND

The City’s Traffic Signal and Streetlight Division maintains about 18,000 streetlight poles,
which are vital for public safety and transportation. When poles are damaged, often due
to collisions or vandalism, quick replacement is necessary to maintain visibility, pedestrian
safety, and meet lighting standards.

Over the past year, approximately 65 poles were replaced. All replacement poles and
parts must meet City specifications to ensure consistency, structural strength, and
compatibility with the existing system.

DISCUSSION

To support the need for commercial streetlight poles, the City issued Invitation for Bid No.
24-001-3220 on February 14, 2024. Two bids were received, and Morgan Ingland LLC
was identified as the lowest responsive bidder. On June 26, 2024, the City Council
 Report to Mayor Pro Tem and City Council

approved a $227,487 purchase order for Fiscal Year 2024–25. The contract includes two
optional one-year extensions.

Staff recommends exercising the first extension for Fiscal Year 2025–26. Maintaining a
ready inventory of streetlight poles and single-arm assemblies helps reduce outage times
and safety risks. Extending the contract with Morgan Ingland LLC ensures continued
supply and helps manage long manufacturing lead times.

$241,080; Sufficient funds for the requisition and resulting purchase order with Morgan
Ingland LLC are budgeted in the Street Light Assessment District supply accounts.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Accept the NOC for PN 698, ATP Avenue R Complete Streets Project; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager Pro Tem or his designee to file the NOC and release
  the security for the completed public street improvements.

BACKGROUND

The Avenue R Complete Streets project is located on Avenue R between Sierra
Highway and 25th Street East. The project’s improvements included widen and
resurfaced 3.48 lane miles of Avenue R, constructed 442,000 square feet of new
sidewalk, installed approximately 5 miles of new Class II Bicycle Lanes with bike-lane
conflict striping, traffic signal modifications, installed 110 new LED streetlights,
constructing 15 new Americans with Disabilities Act compliant curb ramps, installed 38
new driveways, and approximately 3,440 linear feet of new storm drains.

DISCUSSION

The NOC is presented by Section 16.110.060 of Palmdale’s Municipal Code. This action
will accept the roadway improvements as complete and initiate the City’s release of
applicable securities posted for this project by the City’s subdivision regulations.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:
  1. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2025-052, a Resolution of the City Council of the City of

  Collective; and,

  2. Authorize staff to proceed with the full implementation of the new municipal brand

BACKGROUND

The City of Palmdale’s current logo has been in use since 2002. Over the past two
decades, the City has experienced major shifts in population, infrastructure, and regional
influence. However, the City’s visual identity has remained unchanged, limiting its
effectiveness in conveying a cohesive, modern, and recognizable brand image.

To address this, the City entered into a professional services agreement with Hub
Collective in August 2024 to lead a full rebranding initiative. Hub Collective facilitated a
structured process of discovery, engagement, design, and refinement. Public outreach
included:

    488 community survey responses;
    149 staff survey responses;
    Engagements with the Teen Advisory Board, Legacy Commons for Active Seniors,
  Visit Palmdale Board, South Antelope Valley Emergency Services (SAVES),
  departmental leadership, and the City Council; and,
    In-person outreach at Jolly Holiday, reaching more than 200 attendees.

The resulting brand system is based on this diverse and inclusive feedback, positioning
Palmdale for a more unified and forward-looking public identity.

DISCUSSION

The selected final logo, titled “Open Landscape,” features a stylized Joshua tree — a
familiar and beloved symbol of Palmdale’s high desert landscape. The design was the
highest-rated concept among all options presented, receiving 65% favorable staff
responses and 60% favorable community responses.

Survey feedback emphasized the design’s strengths, describing it as:

    “Clean, simple, and playful”;
    “Grounded in place”; and,
    “Optimistic and welcoming”

The logo is paired with the brand tagline: “Community – Innovation – Opportunity”

This message, shaped by stakeholder priorities, conveys the City’s identity as a
resilient, dynamic, and opportunity-rich community.

The design replaces the existing 2002-era logo with a modern, scalable identity that is
suitable for both digital and print applications. The full brand system includes a toolkit
provided by Hub Collective, consisting of logo files, typography, iconography, color
palettes, templates, and usage guidelines. This identity will be implemented in a phased
approach to ensure cost efficiency and operational flexibility.

FISCAL IMPACT

No new appropriation is required at this time. Through the annual budget process, the
City Council approved $500,000 to support the early stages of implementing the City’s
new brand identity. These funds will be used for initial activities such as applying the
brand, design support, and some physical updates. The rollout of the new brand identity
will occur in phases, starting with digital and low- or no-cost assets like website elements,
social media profiles, email signatures, and internal templates.

Physical updates—such as signage, vehicle decals, uniforms, and printed materials—will

As individual branding applications are developed—such as facility signage, gateway

F. Forfeiture. Should any Committee member miss three (3) consecutive

  Committee meetings without any prior consent or notice to the Committee, they

  shall forfeit their membership on the Committee. All forfeited Committee positions

  shall be subject to Article II, Section E, for the purpose of their vacancy.

G. Chair. The Committee shall appoint one member to serve as the Chair of the

  Committee by a simple majority vote. The Chair shall preside over all meetings of

  the Committee. The Chair is responsible for keeping order and decorum during

  the Committee’s meetings.

H. Vice-Chair. The Committee shall appoint one member to serve as the Vice-Chair

  of the Committee by simple majority vote. The Vice-Chair shall perform the duties

  of the Chair in the absence or incapacity of the Chair, until such time as a new

  Chair is selected or appointed. Should both the Chair and Vice-Chair be absent

  or incapacitated, the Committee shall vote by simple majority to appoint an

  interim Chair and Vice-Chair for the purpose of that current meeting and any
   subsequent meetings until either the Chair or Vice-Chair are able to return to

  their duties.

  I. Staff Secretary. City staff shall appoint one member to serve as the Staff

  Secretary of the Committee. The Staff Secretary shall keep the minutes of all

  official meetings of the Committee, which shall be open for inspection by any

  member of the public. The Staff Secretary shall sign reports and correspondence

  for the Committee, along with setting meeting dates; providing agendas to each

  Committee member prior to each official meeting. The Staff Secretary shall

  inform Committee members of all available data gathered by City staff pertinent

  to each item on said agenda. The Staff Secretary shall inform Committee

  members of the time and place of any special meeting. The Staff Secretary shall

  make available to the Committee all correspondence addressed to the

  Committee.

ARTICLE III – MEETINGS

  A. Rules. All meetings will fall under rules set by the Ralph M. Brown Act (Cal. Gov’t

  Code §54950 et seq.) (“Brown Act”).

  B. Meeting Dates. The Measure AV Oversight Committee shall meet bi-monthly

  (i.e., every two (2) months), and as needed, to carry out its purpose. These set

  dates can be changed by resolution as needed.

  C. Specials Meetings and Emergency. Special Meetings can be called by the

  Chair or Vice Chair with five days prior notice. Emergency meetings can be

  called as needed.
   D. Open and Public Meetings. All meetings concerning all Committee actions and

  deliberations shall be open and allow for anyone in the public to attend.

  E. Agenda. An agenda shall be published to the public and sent out to each

  Committee member no less than seventy-two (72) hours before the meeting

  takes place. All agendas should include time, date, and location where the

  meeting(s) are to take place along with the type of meeting (Regular, Special, or

  Emergency). Any items not on the agenda will be placed in the non-agenda items

  portion of the meeting.

  F. Minutes. The minutes of the Committee's proceedings and all documents

  received and reports issued shall be a matter of public record and made

  available on an Internet website maintained by the Committee.

ARTICLE IV. – CONDUCT OF MEETINGS
  A. Order of Business. The regular order of business shall be:

  1. Call to Order

  2. Public Comment

  3. Approval of Minutes from the previous meeting.

  4. Consideration and Action of Agenda Items

  5. Non-Agenda Items

  6. Adjournment

  The order of business can be modified as needed.

  B. Parliamentary Procedure. All proceedings before the Committee may be guided

  by the rules of parliamentary procedure set forth in Rosenberg’s Rules of Order,
   but failure to follow Rosenberg’s Rules of Order shall not affect the validity of any

  action or motion duly taken or adopted by the Committee at any lawfully held

  meeting.

  C. Presentations to the Committee. Any person desiring to address the

  Committee shall be requested, when recognized by the Chair, to give his or her

  name and address for the record. The Chair may, in the interest of facilitating the

  business of the Committee, set in advance of the presentation of testimony

  reasonable time limits for oral presentations. Persons may be required to submit

  written testimony in lieu of oral testimony if the Chair determines that a

  reasonable opportunity for oral presentations has been provided, and in such a

  case, the matter may be continued to a later date to allow a reasonable time for

  such submittals to occur.

  D. Attendance. Members shall be considered present at the Committee meeting if

  they are there physically, on the phone, or using a video conferencing

  application.

ARTICLE V. – VOTING AND QUORUM

  A. Roll Call Vote. A roll call vote may be required in voting upon any motion of the

  Committee at the discretion of the Chair.

  B. Quorum. A majority of the currently appointed members of the Committee shall

  constitute a quorum for the purpose of conducting its business and exercising its

  powers and for all other official purposes, except that less than a quorum may

  adjourn from time to time until a quorum is obtained.
 C. Number of Votes Required for Action. All actions require a motion and a

second. No action or recommendation of the Committee shall be valid and binding

unless a quorum is present, and the motion is approved by a simple majority of the

members present. Each member shall have one vote. No votes may be cast by

proxy. Tie votes shall be considered as denial of the motion.

D. Conflicts of Interest. The Committee shall be subject to conflict of interest in

accordance with the Fair Political Practices Act. City Councilpersons shall not vote

for any person who presents a conflict of interest with them.

E. Motion to Reconsider. The Committee may reconsider a matter during the

meeting at which the vote was taken, provided all members who were present when

the matter was discussed and voted upon are still present, all persons who

addressed the Committee regarding the matter are still present, and the motion to

reconsider is made by a member who voted with the prevailing side. A motion for

reconsideration shall have precedence over every motion except a motion to

adjourn. A final vote on any matter may also be placed on any future agenda for

reconsideration by the Committee or any member of the Committee at the meeting

at which the action was taken or at any later time. Any interested person may

request that an action be reconsidered, provided that such a request must be in

writing and filed with the Palmdale City Clerk within ten calendar days of the action

of the Committee.
 ARTICLE VI. - AMENDMENTS.

  Any amendment to these Bylaws shall be approved by a simple majority vote of the

  entire Committee and ratified by the City Council.

BACKGROUND

On September 21, 2022, Palmdale 2045 was adopted by the City Council and replaced
the previously adopted General Plan (1993). State law requires that the regulations
governing the use and development of lands within the municipal limits of a city be
consistent with the adopted General Plan for that city. ZOA 21-007 was adopted by the
City Council on March 15, 2023, which amended Title 17 of the Palmdale Municipal Code
(PMC) to implement the vision of Palmdale 2045 as well as support new land use patterns
and future development. Since then, staff have identified minor amendments to Title 17,

On June 12, 2025, the Planning Commission adopted Resolution No. PC-2025-012
recommending City Council approval of ZOA 25-0001.

DISCUSSION

The Planning Commission recommends City Council approval of the proposed
amendments to the detached single-family residential development standards to allow
the use of foam trim around exterior doors, windows, and decorative features. Foam trim
is a widely used decorative material in the construction of single-family homes, and this
amendment will provide developers with additional flexibility in materials while ensuring
high-quality aesthetics.

The proposed amendment also addresses ADUs within the multi-family residential
standards to comply with State law. Local agencies cannot mandate replacement parking
when an uncovered parking space is demolished during the construction or conversion
of an ADU (Gov. Code § 66314, subdivisions (d)(11)). Additionally, Government Code
Section 66313 has revised the definition of “livable space” to encompass any area in a
dwelling intended for human habitation, including living, sleeping, eating, cooking, or
sanitation. Furthermore, the maximum number of allowed detached ADUs for lots with an
existing multi-family dwelling has increased from two to eight, as long as the number of
detached ADUs does not exceed the number of primary dwelling units on the lot.

Approval of the proposed amendments complies with Palmdale 2045, Chapter Five, Land
Use and Community Design, Goal LUD-4, which emphasizes the need for high-quality
architecture and site design in the renovation and construction of all buildings; and, LUD-
22, which encourages the development of neighborhoods with a range of housing
opportunities that allow people of all ages, abilities, socioeconomic status, and family size
to live in Palmdale.

PEIR 22-002 (State Clearinghouse # 2021060494) was prepared and certified by the City
Council (Resolution No. CC 2022-096) on September 21, 2022, for approval of Palmdale
